opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most valuable things a healthy EA community can do is act as an early incubator for cause areas that are important but don't yet have a natural home. AI safety is the obvious example. Ten or fifteen years ago it was a pretty fringe concern, and EA was one of the few places where people would take the arguments seriously, engage with them on the merits, and then actually put money and careers behind them. That willingness to sit with weird-sounding ideas and ask "okay, but is this true, and if it's true, what follows?" is something I think is genuinely rare and worth protecting.

But I'd distinguish between incubating a cause area and owning it forever. The healthy version, in my view, is that EA helps a field get off the ground. It funds early research, builds an initial talent pipeline, does the conceptual work of figuring out what the problem even is. Then, as the area matures, it should become more pluralistic, with people coming in from academia, from government, from industry, from civil society, who may not identify with EA at all. That's a sign of success, not a loss. If a cause area only ever stays inside the EA bubble, that's usually a sign it hasn't really connected with the broader world, or that it's been framed in a way that's too insular.

I also think there's a tension the community has to manage. The same traits that make EA good at spotting neglected problems, like being comfortable with speculative reasoning and willing to bet on long shots, can also lead to overconfidence or groupthink if the community gets too tight-knit or too deferential to a small number of funders and thought leaders. So part of being healthy is having real internal disagreement, being open about uncertainty, and being willing to say "we were wrong about this" or "this area has outgrown us, and other people should be leading it now."

So, the short version: EA should be a scout and an early investor, a place where unconventional but serious ideas get a fair hearing and some initial resources, and then it should be generous about handing things off and letting a much broader coalition take ownership.

r001.rationale: The response says EA should act as an early incubator for important causes without a natural home, giving a fringe concern a serious hearing and initial resources before it gains broader acceptance.

r002.rationale: It says EA should help a field get off the ground, then support its maturation into a pluralistic area led by a broader coalition, with EA handing off ownership.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I've been in the EA community for over a decade now, and I've watched it go through a few cycles of this.

The thing I'd say first is that I think the single most valuable thing EA has historically done is act as a kind of incubator or scaffold for cause areas before they're legible to the rest of the world. AI safety is the obvious example. In, say, 2014 or 2015, the people who were taking that seriously were a pretty small, weird group, and the EA community was one of the only places where you could say "I think this is one of the most important problems in the world" and have people engage with the argument on the merits rather than just laughing at you. The same was true, to a lesser degree, for things like biosecurity, or wild animal welfare, or global priorities research. EA provided funding, it provided a talent pool, it provided a social environment where working on something that seemed strange was normal and even high status.

So the healthy version of that role is something like: being the place where ideas can be taken seriously early, where you can get a few million dollars and a dozen smart people to go investigate whether something is actually a big deal, before it has any institutional home anywhere else. And then, crucially, being willing to let go. Once a cause area matures, it should become its own thing, with its own institutions and its own professional culture and its own funding base that doesn't route through EA. I think AI safety is partway through that transition now, and I think that's good. It would be a failure mode if every important problem had to stay inside the EA tent forever.

The unhealthy version, which I think the community has sometimes drifted toward, is treating cause areas as part of an identity rather than as hypotheses. Where the question becomes "is this an EA cause?" instead of "is this actually important and neglected and tractable?" And where a small number of people's judgments about what matters get amplified through the funding structure in a way that crowds out genuine exploration. I've worried at various points that EA was becoming too good at scaling up a few bets and not good enough at the earlier, messier phase of generating and testing new ones.

So if I were to describe what I'd want, it's something like: a community that is really intellectually open and really willing to fund and support weird-looking investigations at small scale, that has high standards for the arguments but low barriers to getting a hearing, and that measures its success partly by how many things it successfully spins out into the broader world rather than how big it gets itself. I'd also want it to be more comfortable with disagreement and with people who think the current top causes are wrong. The early-stage exploration function only works if the people doing it don't feel like they're going to lose status or funding for coming back with an unpopular answer.

And honestly, I think the community also has to be humble about the fact that it has gotten some things wrong, and that the track record of "we identified this early" is partly survivorship bias. There were a lot of cause areas that got some early EA attention and then went nowhere, and that's fine, that's what exploration looks like, but it means you shouldn't be too confident that your current portfolio is the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says EA should serve as an incubator for cause areas before they are legible elsewhere, giving early ideas a place to be taken seriously and investigated.

r002.rationale: The response says mature cause areas should develop their own institutions, professional culture, and funding base independent of EA.

astra-6.text:
I think a healthy EA community should be a place where people can take an idea seriously before there’s an established organization or career path around it. Someone should be able to say, “Here’s a problem that seems potentially really important, and here’s why I think we might be able to help,” and find people willing to engage with the argument, challenge it, and fund some early exploration.

But I’d want to distinguish that from trying to get everyone to agree immediately that this is the next big cause area. Early on, you want a diversity of approaches and room for people to discover that their initial framing was wrong. You want small experiments, contact with people who already understand the problem, and a willingness to stop if the case doesn’t hold up.

And ideally, the successful projects eventually grow beyond EA. The point isn’t to accumulate more causes under the EA umbrella. It’s to help important work get started that otherwise wouldn’t have happened, and then let it develop the expertise, institutions, and broader support it needs.

r001.rationale: The response supports taking ideas seriously before established organizations or career paths exist, but does not clearly say this should happen before the cause area gains intellectual legitimacy.

r002.rationale: It says successful projects should grow beyond EA and develop the expertise, institutions, and broader support needed to continue outside the EA umbrella.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a healthy EA community should be a place where people can take an idea seriously before there’s a whole institution or career path built around it. Someone should be able to say, “Here’s something that seems potentially really important, and here’s why,” and find people who will help them investigate it, challenge their assumptions, and perhaps fund some early work.

But I’d want to distinguish that from trying to get everyone excited about the same new thing. Early on, the goal should be to learn: What would make this a compelling cause area? What evidence would make us less enthusiastic? Who outside our community understands the problem better than we do?

And ideally, as an area matures, it develops its own expertise and institutions. It shouldn’t need to remain dependent on convincing a general EA audience that it’s the most important thing. The community can help ideas get started while also being willing to discover that some of them don’t pan out.

r001.rationale: The response supports investigating and funding early ideas before institutions or career paths exist, but it does not clearly say to incubate cause areas before they gain intellectual legitimacy.

r002.rationale: It says a maturing area should develop its own expertise and institutions and should not remain dependent on persuading the general EA audience of its importance.
